studies.title: Anterior cingulate cortex grey matter volume abnormalities in adolescents with PTSD after childhood sexual abuse.
studies.abstract: Adverse childhood experiences (ACE) substantially increase the risk of later psychiatric and somatic pathology. While neurobiological factors are likely to play a mediating role, specific insights are lacking. The scarce neuroimaging studies in traumatised pediatric populations have provided inconsistent results, potentially due to the inclusion of different types of trauma. To further improve our understanding of the neurobiology of pediatric psychotrauma, this study seeks to investigate abnormalities in grey matter volume (GMV) in a homogeneous group of adolescents with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) due to childhood sexual abuse (CSA) and the relationship between GMV and symptom severity. We performed a voxel based morphometry (VBM) analysis in 21 adolescents with CSA-related PTSD and 25 matched non-traumatised, non-clinical adolescents. Hippocampus, amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), medial PFC (mPFC) and superior temporal gyrus (STG) were chosen as regions of interest (ROIs). Trauma symptomatology was measured with the Trauma Symptom Checklist for Children (TSCC) and dissociation symptoms with the Adolescent Dissociative Experiences Scale (A-DES). The ROI analysis showed that the CSA-related PTSD group had significant smaller volumes of the dorsal ACC as compared to healthy controls. However, no correlations were found between GMV and scores on the TSCC and A-DES. The smaller ACC volume is partly in line with previous studies in traumatised youth and is a consistent finding in traumatised adults. Taken together our results suggest that the dorsal ACC is implicated in the neurobiological sequelae of CSA, potentially associated with an altered evaluative processing of emotion, but not directly with PTSD severity.

Measures of intracranial tissue volume and cerebral tissue volume have been observed to be smaller in adolescents with maltreatment-related PTSD. Second, lower intelligence, a risk factor for PTSD, is associated with smaller cerebral tissue volumes. Nevertheless, to our knowledge, only 1 study has observed globally smaller cerebral tissue volume in adults with PTSD.

studies.title: Decreased premotor cortex volume in victims of urban violence with posttraumatic stress disorder.
studies.abstract: Studies addressing posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) have demonstrated that PTSD patients exhibit structural abnormalities in brain regions that relate to stress regulation and fear responses, such as the hippocampus, amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex, and ventromedial prefrontal cortex. Premotor cortical areas are involved in preparing to respond to a threatening situation and in representing the peripersonal space. Urban violence is an important and pervasive cause of human suffering, especially in large urban centers in the developing world. Violent events, such as armed robbery, are very frequent in certain cities, and these episodes increase the risk of PTSD. Assaultive trauma is characterized by forceful invasion of the peripersonal space; therefore, could this traumatic event be associated with structural alteration of premotor areas in PTSD?

studies.title: Frontal and subcortical grey matter reductions in PTSD.
studies.abstract: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is characterised by a range of debilitating psychological, physical and cognitive symptoms. PTSD has been associated with grey matter atrophy in limbic and frontal cortical brain regions. However, previous studies have reported heterogeneous findings, with grey matter changes observed beyond limbic/frontal areas. Seventy-five adults were recruited from the community, 25 diagnosed with PTSD along with 25 healthy and 25 trauma exposed age and gender matched controls. Participants underwent clinical assessment and magnetic resonance imaging. The data-analyses method Voxel Based Morphometry (VBM) was used to estimate cortical grey matter volumes. When compared to both healthy and trauma exposed controls, PTSD subjects demonstrated decreased grey matter volumes within subcortical brain regions-including the hippocampus and amygdala-along with reductions in the anterior cingulate cortex, frontal medial cortex, middle frontal gyrus, superior frontal gyrus, paracingulate gyrus, and precuneus cortex. Significant negative correlations were found between total CAPS lifetime clinical scores/sub-scores and GM volume of both the PTSD and TC groups. GM volumes of the left rACC and right amygdala showed a significant negative correlation within PTSD diagnosed subjects.

studies.title: A transdiagnostic neuroanatomical signature of psychiatric illness.
studies.abstract: Despite an increasing focus on transdiagnostic approaches to mental health, it remains unclear whether different diagnostic categories share a common neuronatomical basis. The current investigation sought to investigate whether a transdiagnostic set of structural alterations characterized schizophrenia, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder, and determine whether any such alterations reflected markers of psychiatric illness or pre-existing familial vulnerability. A total of 404 patients with a psychiatric diagnosis were recruited (psychosis, n = 129; unipolar depression, n = 92; post-traumatic stress disorder, n = 91; obsessive-compulsive disorder, n = 92) alongside n = 201 healthy controls and n = 20 unaffected first-degree relatives. We collected structural magnetic resonance imaging scans from each participant, and tested for transdiagnostic alterations using Voxel-based morphometry. Inferences were made at p < 0.05 after family-wise error correction for multiple comparisons. The four psychiatric groups relative to healthy controls were all characterized by significantly greater gray matter volume in the putamen (right: z-score: 5.97, p-value < 0.001; left: z-score: 4.97, p-value = 0.001); the volume of this region was positively correlated with severity of symptoms across groups (r = 0.313; p < 0.001). Putamen enlargement was also evident in unaffected relatives compared to healthy controls (right: z-score: 8.13, p-value < 0.001; left: z-score: 9.38, p-value < 0.001). Taken collectively, these findings indicate that increased putamen volume may reflect a transdiagnostic marker of familial vulnerability to psychopathology. This is consistent with emerging conceptualizations of psychiatric illness, in which each disorder is understood as a combination of diagnosis-specific features and a transdiagnostic factor reflecting general psychopathology.

studies.title: Abnormal structure of fear circuitry in pediatric post-traumatic stress disorder.
studies.abstract: Structural brain studies of adult post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) show reduced gray matter volume (GMV) in fear regulatory areas including the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and hippocampus. Surprisingly, neither finding has been reported in pediatric PTSD. One possibility is that they represent age-dependent effects that are not fully apparent until adulthood. In addition, lower-resolution MRI and image processing in prior studies may have limited detection of such differences. Here we examine fear circuitry GMV, including age-related differences, using higher-resolution MRI in pediatric PTSD vs healthy youth. In a cross-sectional design, 3 T anatomical brain MRI was acquired in 27 medication-free youth with PTSD and 27 healthy non-traumatized youth of comparable age, sex, and IQ. Voxel-based morphometry was used to compare GMV in a priori regions including the medial prefrontal cortex and amygdala/hippocampus. Compared with healthy youth, PTSD youth had reduced GMV but no age-related differences in anterior vmPFC (BA 10/11, Z=4.5), which inversely correlated with PTSD duration. In contrast, although there was no overall group difference in hippocampal volume, a group × age interaction (Z=3.6) was present in the right anterior hippocampus. Here, age positively predicted hippocampal volume in healthy youth but negatively predicted volume in PTSD youth. Within the PTSD group, re-experiencing symptoms inversely correlated with subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC, Z=3.7) and right anterior hippocampus (Z=3.5) GMV. Pediatric PTSD is associated with abnormal structure of the vmPFC and age-related differences in the hippocampus, regions important in the extinction and contextual gating of fear. Reduced anterior vmPFC volume may confer impaired recovery from illness, consistent with its role in the allocation of attentional resources. In contrast, individual differences in sgACC volume were associated with re-experiencing symptoms, consistent with the role of the sgACC in fear extinction. The negative relationship between age and hippocampal volume in youth with PTSD may suggest an ongoing neurotoxic process over development, which further contributes to illness expression. Future studies employing a longitudinal design would be merited to further explore these possibilities.

studies.title: Duration of posttraumatic stress disorder predicts hippocampal grey matter loss.
studies.abstract: To examine the impact of environmental stress on grey matter volume in posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), we investigated the relationship between duration of PTSD and grey matter volume of hippocampus and anterior cingulate cortex. Twenty-one participants with PTSD and 17 trauma-exposed controls, matched for age and sex and with no history of substance dependence, underwent a T1-weighted structural MRI scan and voxel-based morphometry was employed. After controlling for age, depression and whole-brain volume, analysis of covariance revealed significant reductions in hippocampus and rostral anterior cingulate cortex in PTSD, and there was a significant negative correlation between right hippocampal volume and PTSD duration. This pattern suggests that prolonged PTSD may have cumulative adverse effects on hippocampal volume, highlighting the potential role of genetic-environmental interactions.

studies.title: Effects of post-traumatic stress disorder on occipital lobe function and structure.
studies.abstract: Although there is evidence for strong connectivity between the amygdala and the visual cortex and some evidence for reduced occipital lobe gray matter volume in patients with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), few studies have directly examined the effects of PTSD on occipital function. The current study used functional and structural MRI to examine occipital cortex function and structure in male combat veterans with and without PTSD. Left occipital gray matter volume was reduced in PTSD patients relative to the controls and correlated negatively with the severity of PTSD symptoms. Functional activity in the lateral occipital complex to aversive and nonaversive pictures presented in novel and repeated presentations was not altered by PTSD. These findings suggest that PTSD adversely affects occipital lobe volume but not the reactivity of the lateral occipital complex to generally aversive, trauma nonspecific stimuli.

studies.title: Post-traumatic stress symptoms correlate with smaller subgenual cingulate, caudate, and insula volumes in unmedicated combat veterans.
studies.abstract: Prior studies have examined differences in brain volume between patients with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and control subjects. Convergent findings include smaller hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex volumes in PTSD. However, post-traumatic stress symptoms (PTSS) exist on a spectrum, and neural changes may occur beyond the diagnostic threshold of PTSD. We examined the relationship between PTSS and gray matter among combat-exposed U.S. military veterans. Structural brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was obtained on 28 combat veterans from Operations Enduring and Iraqi Freedom. PTSS were assessed using the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale (CAPS). Thirteen subjects met criteria for PTSD. Subjects were unmedicated, and free of major comorbid psychiatric disorders. Images were analyzed using voxel-based morphometry, and regressed against the total CAPS score and trauma load. Images were subsequently analyzed by diagnosis of PTSD vs. non-PTSD. studies.title: Voxel-based analysis of MRI reveals anterior cingulate gray-matter volume reduction in posttraumatic stress disorder due to terrorism.
studies.abstract: MRI studies using the manual tracing method have shown a smaller-than-normal hippocampal volume in patients with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). However, these studies have yielded inconsistent results, and brain structures other than the hippocampus have not been well investigated. A recently developed, fully automated method called voxel-based morphometry enables an exploration of structural changes throughout the brain by applying statistical parametric mapping to high-resolution MRI. Here we first used this technology in patients with PTSD. Participants were 9 victims of the Tokyo subway sarin attack with PTSD and 16 matched victims of the same traumatic event without PTSD. The voxel-based morphometry showed a significant gray-matter volume reduction in the left anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) in trauma survivors with PTSD compared with those without PTSD. The severity of the disorder was negatively correlated with the gray-matter volume of the left ACC in PTSD subjects. There were no significant differences in other gray-matter regions or any of the white-matter regions between two groups. The present study demonstrates evidence for structural abnormalities of ACC in patients with PTSD. Together with previous functional neuroimaging studies showing a dysfunction of this region, the present findings provide further support for the important role of ACC, which is pivotally involved in attention, emotional regulation, and conditioned fear, in the pathology of PTSD.

studies.abstract: The neurobiological basis of cancer-related post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) has never been studied. We investigated brain structural alterations and the longitudinal courses in patients with cancer-related PTSD. Baseline scans using magnetic resonance imaging were performed in 14 cancer survivors with PTSD, 100 without PTSD, and 70 healthy subjects. Follow-up scans were performed 2 years later in 76 cancer survivors (PTSD, n=9; non-PTSD, n=67). Using voxel-based morphometry, the gray matter volume (GMV) of the cancer survivors with PTSD was compared with the GMVs of those without PTSD and of the healthy subjects. The effects of the interactions between the diagnosis and the timing of the GMV measurements were examined. The GMV of the right orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) was significantly smaller in cancer survivors with PTSD than in those without PTSD or healthy subjects. The interaction between the diagnosis and the timing of the right OFC's GMV measurement was not significant. The OFC, which is thought to be involved in the extinction of fear conditioning and the retrieval of emotional memory, might play an important role in the pathophysiology of PTSD. Moreover, the OFC's GMV may remain constant after the development of cancer-related PTSD.

studies.title: Gray matter density in limbic and paralimbic cortices is associated with trauma load and EMDR outcome in PTSD patients.
studies.abstract: There is converging evidence of gray matter (GM) structural alterations in different limbic structures in Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) patients. The aim of this study was to evaluate GM density in PTSD in relation to trauma load, and to assess the GM differences between responders (R) and non-responders (NR) to EMDR therapy. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans of 21 subjects exposed to occupational trauma, who developed PTSD (S), and of 22 who did not (NS), were compared by means of an optimized Voxel-Based Morphometry (VBM) analysis as implemented in SPM. Within S, further comparisons were made between 10 R and 5 NR. A regression analysis between GM density and the Traumatic Antecedents Questionnaire (TAQ) was also performed on all 43 subjects. Results showed a significantly lower GM density in S as compared to NS in the left posterior cingulate and the left posterior parahippocampal gyrus. Moreover, NR showed a significantly lower GM density as compared to R in bilateral posterior cingulate, as well as anterior insula, anterior parahippocampal gyrus and amygdala in the right hemisphere. Regression analysis showed that GM density negatively correlated with trauma load in bilateral posterior cingulate, left anterior insula, and right anterior parahippocampal gyrus. In conclusion, a GM lower density in limbic and paralimbic cortices were found to be associated with PTSD diagnosis, trauma load, and EMDR treatment outcome, suggesting a view of PTSD characterized by memory and dissociative disturbances.

studies.title: Decreased gray matter volume in the left hippocampus and bilateral calcarine cortex in coal mine flood disaster survivors with recent onset PTSD.
studies.abstract: Although limbic structure changes have been found in chronic and recent onset post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) patients, there are few studies about brain structure changes in recent onset PTSD patients after a single extreme and prolonged trauma. In the current study, 20 coal mine flood disaster survivors underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and region of interest (ROI) techniques were used to detect the gray matter and white matter volume changes in 10 survivors with recent onset PTSD and 10 survivors without PTSD. The correlation between the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale (CAPS) and gray matter density in the ROI was also studied. Compared with survivors without PTSD, survivors with PTSD had significantly decreased gray matter volume and density in left anterior hippocampus, left parahippocampal gyrus, and bilateral calcarine cortex. The CAPS score correlated negatively with the gray matter density in bilateral calcarine cortex and left hippocampus in coal mine disaster survivors. Our study suggests that the gray matter volume and density of limbic structure decreased in recent onset PTSD patients who were exposed to extreme trauma. PTSD symptom severity was associated with gray matter density in calcarine cortex and hippocampus.

studies.title: Converging evidence for abnormalities of the prefrontal cortex and evaluation of midsagittal structures in pediatric posttraumatic stress disorder: an MRI study.
studies.abstract: Volumetric imaging research has shown abnormal brain morphology in posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) when compared with control subjects. We present results on a study of brain morphology in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and midline structures, via indices of gray matter volume and density, in pediatric PTSD. We hypothesized that both methods would demonstrate aberrant morphology in the PFC. Further, we hypothesized aberrant brainstem anatomy and reduced corpus callosum volume in children with PTSD. Twenty-four children (aged 7-14) with history of interpersonal trauma and 24 age- and gender-matched controls underwent structural magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI). Images of the PFC and midline brain structures were first analyzed using volumetric image analysis. The PFC data were then compared with whole brain voxel-based techniques using statistical parametric mapping (SPM). The PTSD group showed significantly increased gray matter volume in the right and left inferior and superior quadrants of the PFC and smaller gray matter volume in the pons and posterior vermis areas by volumetric image analysis. The voxel-by-voxel group comparisons demonstrated increased gray matter density mostly localized to ventral PFC as compared with the control group. Abnormal frontal lobe morphology, as revealed by separate-complementary image analysis methods, and reduced pons and posterior vermis areas are associated with pediatric PTSD. Voxel-based morphometry may help to corroborate and further localize data obtained by volume of interest methods in PTSD.

studies.title: Evidence of diffuse damage in frontal and occipital cortex in the brain of patients with post-traumatic stress disorder.
studies.abstract: A number of MRI studies have shown focal or diffuse cortical gray matter (GM) abnormalities in patients with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). However, the results of these studies are unclear regarding the cortical regions involved in this condition, perhaps due to the heterogeneity of the PTSD population included or to the differences in the methodology used for the quantification of the brain structures. In this study, we assessed differences in cortical GM volumes between a selected group of 25 drug-naive PTSD patients with history of adulthood trauma and 25 matched non-traumatized controls. Analyses were performed by using two different automated methods: the structural image evaluation using normalization of atrophy (SIENAX) and the voxel-based morphometry (VBM), as we trusted that if these complementary techniques provided similar results, it would increase the confidence in the validity of the assessment. Results of SIENAX and VBM analyses similarly showed that cortical GM volume decreases in PTSD patients when compared to healthy controls, particularly in the frontal and occipital lobes. These decreases seem to correlate with clinical measures. Our findings suggest that in drug-naïve PTSD patients with a history of adulthood trauma, brain structural damage is diffuse, with a particular prevalence for the frontal and occipital lobes, and is clinically relevant.

studies.title: Gray matter density reduction in the insula in fire survivors with posttraumatic stress disorder: a voxel-based morphometric study.
studies.abstract: Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) is an objective whole-brain technique for characterizing regional cerebral volume and tissue concentration differences in structural magnetic resonance images. In the current study, we used VBM to examine possible cerebral gray matter abnormalities in patients with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) due to fire. The subjects included 12 victims of a fire disaster with PTSD and 12 matched victims of the same fire without PTSD. Magnetic resonance images were obtained on a 1.5-Tesla General Electric scanner at Central South University, and an entire brain volume of 248 contiguous slices was obtained for each subject. Then, gray matter density in patients with PTSD and control groups was compared by using a VBM approach in SPM2. Group analysis was thresholded at P<0.001, uncorrected, at the voxel level. The following three regions of reduced gray matter volume were found in patients with PTSD compared with controls: left hippocampus, left anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and bilateral insular cortex. It was concluded that there are structural abnormalities of the hippocampus, the ACC and the insular cortex in patients with PTSD due to fire.

studies.title: Characterizing Typhoon-related Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Based on Multimodal Fusion of Structural, Diffusion, and Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
studies.abstract: Diagnosing posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) using only single-modality images is controversial. We aimed to use multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) combining structural, diffusion, and functional MRI to possibly provide a more comprehensive viewpoint on the decisive characteristics of PTSD patients. Typhoon-exposed individuals with (n = 26) and without PTSD (n = 32) and healthy volunteers (n = 30) were enrolled. Five MRI features from three modalities, including two resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) features (amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation, ALFF; and regional homogeneity, ReHo), one structural MRI feature (gray matter density, GM), and two diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) features (fractional anisotropy, FA; and mean diffusivity, MD) were investigated simultaneously with a multimodal canonical correlation analysis + joint independent component analysis model to identify abnormalities in the PTSD brain. We identified statistical differences between PTSD patients and healthy controls in terms of 1 rs-fMRI (ALFF, ReHo) alterations in the superior frontal gyrus, precuneus, inferior parietal lobule (IPL), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), 2 DTI (FA, MD) changes in the pons, genu, and splenium of the corpus callosum, and 3 Structural MRI abnormalities in the precuneus, IPL, ACC, and PCC. A novel ReHo component was found to distinguish PTSD and trauma-exposed controls, including the precuneus, IPL, middle frontal gyrus, middle occipital gyrus, and cerebellum. This study reveals that PTSD individuals exhibit intertwined functional and structural anomalies within the default mode network. Some alterations within this network may serve as a potential marker to distinguish between PTSD patients and trauma-exposed controls.

studies.title: Brain morphological changes and functional neuroanatomy related to cognitive and emotional distractors during working memory maintenance in post-traumatic stress disorder.
studies.abstract: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is associated with abnormalities in the processing and regulation of emotion as well as cognitive deficits. This study evaluated the differential brain activation patterns associated with cognitive and emotional distractors during working memory (WM) maintenance for human faces between patients with PTSD and healthy controls (HCs) and assessed the relationship between changes in the activation patterns by the opposing effects of distraction types and gray matter volume (GMV). Twenty-two patients with PTSD and twenty-two HCs underwent T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and event-related functional MRI (fMRI), respectively. Event-related fMRI data were recorded while subjects performed a delayed-response WM task with human face and trauma-related distractors. Compared to the HCs, the patients with PTSD showed significantly reduced GMV of the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) (p < 0.05, FWE-corrected). For the human face distractor trial, the patients showed significantly decreased activities in the superior frontal gyrus and IFG compared with HCs (p < 0.05, FWE-corrected). The patients showed lower accuracy scores and slower reaction times for the face recognition task with trauma-related distractors compared with HCs as well as significantly increased brain activity in the STG during the trauma-related distractor trial was observed (p < 0.05, FWE-corrected). Such differential brain activation patterns associated with the effects of distraction in PTSD patients may be linked to neural mechanisms associated with impairments in both cognitive control for confusable distractors and the ability to control emotional distraction.

studies.title: Volumetric Integrated Classification Index: An Integrated Voxel-Based Morphometry and Machine Learning Interpretable Biomarker for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder.
studies.abstract: PTSD is a complex mental health condition triggered by individuals' traumatic experiences, with long-term and broad impacts on sufferers' psychological health and quality of life. Despite decades of research providing partial understanding of the pathobiological aspects of PTSD, precise neurobiological markers and imaging indicators remain challenging to pinpoint. This study employed VBM analysis and machine learning algorithms to investigate structural brain changes in PTSD patients. Data were sourced ADNI-DoD database for PTSD cases and from the ADNI database for healthy controls. Various machine learning models, including SVM, RF, and LR, were utilized for classification. Additionally, the VICI was proposed to enhance model interpretability, incorporating SHAP analysis. The association between PTSD risk genes and VICI values was also explored through gene expression data analysis. Among the tested machine learning algorithms, RF emerged as the top performer, achieving high accuracy in classifying PTSD patients. Structural brain abnormalities in PTSD patients were predominantly observed in prefrontal areas compared to healthy controls. The proposed VICI demonstrated classification efficacy comparable to the optimized RF model, indicating its potential as a simplified diagnostic tool. Analysis of gene expression data revealed significant associations between PTSD risk genes and VICI values, implicating synaptic integrity and neural development regulation. This study reveals neuroimaging and genetic characteristics of PTSD, highlighting the potential of VBM analysis and machine learning models in diagnosis and prognosis. The VICI offers a promising approach to enhance model interpretability and guide clinical decision-making. These findings contribute to a better understanding of the pathophysiological mechanisms of PTSD and provide new avenues for future diagnosis and treatment.

studies.title: Changes in brain anatomy during the course of posttraumatic stress disorder.
studies.abstract: The goal of this study was to determine whether posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) was associated with an increase in time-related decline in macrostructural brain volume and whether these changes were associated with accelerated cognitive decline. To quantify brain structure, three-dimensional T1-weighted MRI scans were performed at baseline and again after a minimum of 24months in 25 patients with PTSD (PTSD+) and 22 controls (PTSD-). Longitudinal changes in brain volume were measured using deformation morphometry. For the group as a whole, PTSD+ patients did not show significant ongoing brain atrophy compared to PTSD-. PTSD+ patients were then subgrouped into those with decreasing or increasing symptoms. We found little evidence for brain markers of accelerated atrophy in PTSD+ veterans whose symptoms improved over time, with only a small left parietal region showing greater ongoing tissue loss than PTSD-. PTSD patients whose symptoms increased over time showed accelerated atrophy throughout the brain, particularly brainstem and frontal and temporal lobes. Lastly, for the sample as a whole, greater rates of brain atrophy were associated with greater rates of decline in verbal memory and delayed facial recognition.

studies.title: Amygdala, Hippocampus, and Ventral Medial Prefrontal Cortex Volumes Differ in Maltreated Youth with and without Chronic Posttraumatic Stress Disorder.
studies.abstract: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is considered a disorder of recovery where individuals fail to learn and retain extinction of the traumatic fear response. In maltreated youth, PTSD is common, chronic, and associated with comorbidity. Studies of extinction-related structural volumes (amygdala, hippocampus, anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and ventral medial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC)) and this stress diathesis, in maltreated youth were not previously investigated. In this cross-sectional study, neuroanatomical volumes associated with extinction in maltreated youth with PTSD (N=31), without PTSD (N=32), and in non-maltreated healthy volunteers (n=57) were examined using magnetic resonance imaging. Groups were sociodemographically similar. Participants underwent extensive assessments for strict inclusion/exclusion criteria and DSM-IV disorders. Maltreated youth with PTSD demonstrated decreased right vmPFC volumes compared with both maltreated youth without PTSD and non-maltreated controls. Maltreated youth without PTSD demonstrated larger left amygdala and right hippocampal volumes compared with maltreated youth with PTSD and non-maltreated control youth. PTSD symptoms inversely correlated with right and left hippocampal and left amygdala volumes. Confirmatory masked voxel base morphometry analyses demonstrated greater medial orbitofrontal cortex gray matter intensity in controls than maltreated youth with PTSD. Volumetric results were not influenced by psychopathology or maltreatment variables. We identified volumetric differences in extinction-related structures between maltreated youth with PTSD from those without PTSD. Alterations of the vmPFC may be one mechanism that mediates the pathway from PTSD to comorbidity. Further longitudinal work is needed to determine neurobiological factors related to chronic and persistent PTSD, and to PTSD resilience despite maltreatment.

studies.title: Reduced amygdala volume is associated with deficits in inhibitory control: a voxel- and surface-based morphometric analysis of comorbid PTSD/mild TBI.
studies.abstract: A significant portion of previously deployed combat Veterans from Operation Enduring Freedom and Operation Iraqi Freedom/Operation New Dawn (OEF/OIF/OND) are affected by comorbid posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Despite this fact, neuroimaging studies investigating the neural correlates of cognitive dysfunction within this population are almost nonexistent, with the exception of research examining the neural correlates of diagnostic PTSD or TBI. The current study used both voxel-based and surface-based morphometry to determine whether comorbid PTSD/mTBI is characterized by altered brain structure in the same regions as observed in singular diagnostic PTSD or TBI. Furthermore, we assessed whether alterations in brain structures in these regions were associated with behavioral measures related to inhibitory control, as assessed by the Go/No-go task, self-reports of impulsivity, and/or PTSD or mTBI symptoms. Results indicate volumetric reductions in the bilateral anterior amygdala in our comorbid PTSD/mTBI sample as compared to a control sample of OEF/OIF Veterans with no history of mTBI and/or PTSD. Moreover, increased volume reduction in the amygdala predicted poorer inhibitory control as measured by performance on the Go/No-go task, increased self-reported impulsivity, and greater symptoms associated with PTSD. These findings suggest that alterations in brain anatomy in OEF/OIF/OND Veterans with comorbid PTSD/mTBI are associated with both cognitive deficits and trauma symptoms related to PTSD.

This is an empirical, English-language structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry comparing PTSD patients (n=21) and trauma-exposed controls (n=17). The paper reports whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrasts (PTSD vs controls) with family-wise error correction and provides peak coordinates and figures for hippocampus and anterior cingulate findings. Control population includes trauma-exposed controls without PTSD. The full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion (not just abstract/metadata), so fulltext appears complete. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not non-empirical, not a treatment-only/longitudinal without between-group contrasts). Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6.

This is an empirical, English-language structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry (VBM-DARTEL) that includes a PTSD group (n=24) and a trauma-exposed control group (n=29). The paper reports whole-brain voxel-wise analyses from a factorial design (group factor with PTSD, major depression, control) and follow-up between-group contrasts (the methods state individual group comparisons were performed, inclusively masked with the overall group effect), and reports voxel-wise results (tables/figures) comparing clinical groups and controls. Control participants are trauma-exposed without psychiatric disorder. Results include significant whole-brain cluster-level findings (combined clinical groups v. controls) and PTSD-specific voxel-wise correlation analyses with symptom scores. The full text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is provided. Therefore inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5 and I6 are met; no exclusion criteria apply. Full text appears complete.

This study reports voxel-based morphometry comparisons within a PTSD sample (dissociative subtype vs non-dissociative PTSD) and correlations across PTSD patients, but does not include any between-group contrast of PTSD patients versus control participants (healthy or trauma-exposed without PTSD). Therefore it does not meet the review's required between-group PTSD vs control comparison. Exclusion criterion E8 applies (only within-group results without qualifying PTSD vs control contrast). Inclusion criteria I3 and I4 are not met (no PTSD vs control GM volume comparisons or whole-brain PTSD vs control voxel-wise contrasts). Full text appears complete (includes introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is an empirical, English-language structural MRI voxel-based morphometry study comparing GM volume between PTSD patients and control groups (trauma-exposed controls and healthy controls). The paper reports whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrasts (ANOVA and post hoc voxel-wise VBM results, with figures and supplementary tables) showing significant GM reductions in bilateral hippocampus and left lingual gyrus versus healthy controls. Results are presented as voxel-wise analyses and correlations with symptom severity. The study design, methods, results and discussion are present (full text provided). No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, non-empirical, treatment/longitudinal without between-group contrasts, null-only results, or studies not measuring PTSD) are met. Therefore it satisfies inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5 and I6.

Exclusion IDs met: E4 and E7. This is a longitudinal treatment study of combat-related PTSD patients comparing a therapy group to a waiting-list PTSD group; the analyses are region-of-interest (hippocampus and amygdala) with no reported whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrasts of PTSD patients versus healthy or trauma-exposed controls. Inclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs not met: I3 (does not report GM volume comparisons between PTSD patients and an external control group), I4 (no whole-brain voxel-wise PTSD vs control between-group contrast). Full text appears complete and includes methods, results, and discussion; exclusion is based on study design and reported analyses rather than missing information.

This study is excluded because it does not report a whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrast of PTSD patients versus controls. Exclusion criterion met: E8 (study reports only within-group results / regression analyses relating symptom severity to GM volume, rather than a qualifying between-group PTSD vs control contrast). Inclusion criteria met: I5 (qualifying results are reported in figures/tables/coordinates for voxelwise analyses) and I6 (the sample includes trauma-exposed individuals with and without PTSD, an acceptable control population type). Inclusion criteria not met: I3 (does not provide a between-group comparison of GM volume between PTSD patients and controls) and I4 (does not report a whole-brain voxel-wise between-group PTSD vs control contrast). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion present). Therefore the paper must be excluded from the meta-analysis that requires between-group whole-brain contrasts.

This is an empirical, English-language structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry to compare gray matter volume between PTSD patients (n=15) and trauma-exposed non-PTSD controls (n=17). The paper reports whole-brain, voxel-wise between-group contrasts (NS > S and S > NS) and presents significant GMV differences (reductions in PTSD) with coordinates/tables/figures. Control group is trauma-exposed non-PTSD, which is acceptable. No exclusion criteria are met.

This is an empirical, English-language structural MRI study that performed voxel-based morphometry (VBM) with whole-brain, voxel-wise between-group contrasts comparing gray matter volume in PTSD patients versus trauma-exposed controls. The paper reports between-group VBM results (summarized in Table 3) including peak coordinates and cluster descriptions at an uncorrected threshold (P<0.001), and describes the DARTEL-based whole-brain preprocessing and statistical model (age and TIV covariates). Control group consists of trauma-exposed veterans without PTSD. Although between-group VBM findings did not survive FWE correction, the presence of voxel-wise whole-brain contrast results and reported coordinates satisfies the inclusion criteria (I3, I4, I5, I6) for a morphometry meta-analysis. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion). No exclusion criteria apply.

This study reports voxel-based morphometry analyses within a sample of 28 individuals with PTSD relating grey-matter volume to symptom severity (reexperiencing/flashbacks). It does not include any healthy or trauma-exposed control group nor report whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrasts of PTSD patients vs controls. Therefore it does not meet inclusion criteria I3 (MRI study assessing GM volume differences between PTSD patients and controls) and I4 (reports at least one whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrast). Exclusion criterion E8 applies: the study reports only within-group results in PTSD patients without a qualifying between-group contrast. The full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion). Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met: I3, I4. Exclusion criteria met: E8.

This is an original, English-language empirical structural MRI study using whole-brain voxel-based morphometry (VBM) comparing gray matter volume between youths with PTSD and typically developing controls. The paper reports whole-brain voxelwise between-group contrasts with corrected clusters and peak coordinates, and supplementary/figure-based results are provided. Control population (nontraumatized typically developing youths) is appropriate. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion (longitudinal multimodal VBM and RSFC analyses). No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not non-empirical, measures PTSD, reports between-group contrasts, reports significant group differences). Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6 and should be included in the meta-analysis of structural PTSD morphometry.

This is an empirical, English-language structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry that examines gray matter volume in PTSD vs trauma-exposed non-PTSD controls. The paper reports whole-brain, voxel-wise analyses (regression of CAPS and a voxel-wise group contrast PTSD vs non-PTSD) with peak coordinates and cluster results presented in Table 2 and figures. Controls are trauma-exposed veterans without PTSD, which fits acceptable control populations. The full article text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is provided. Therefore all inclusion criteria relevant to the review are satisfied, and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical English-language MRI study comparing gray matter volumes in maltreated youth with PTSD, maltreated youth without PTSD, and non-maltreated controls (meets I3 and I6). However, the paper does not report any whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrasts (e.g., VBM or other voxel-wise whole-brain GM comparisons). Instead, analyses use parcellation/volumetric regional measures and tractography (region-based/ROI and global volumetry). Therefore it fails I4 (whole-brain voxel-wise evidence) and meets exclusion criterion E4 (ROI-only / no qualifying whole-brain results). Full text appears complete. Inclusion criteria met: I3, I6. Inclusion criteria not met: I4 (no whole-brain voxel-wise GM contrast), I5 (no whole-brain results reported in tables/figures). Exclusion criteria applied: E4.

Although this is an empirical English-language MRI study comparing PTSD patients (n=15) to matched healthy controls and it includes both manual hippocampal volumetry and a whole-brain voxel-wise VBM between-group contrast (satisfying I3, I4, I5, I6), the study reports only null between-group results (no significant GM differences by VBM and no hippocampal volume differences). Per exclusion criterion E9 (studies reporting only null results), this study must be excluded. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion). Inclusion criteria met: I3, I4, I5, I6. Inclusion criteria not met: none. Exclusion criteria met: E9.

This is an empirical, English-language MRI study comparing PTSD patients with trauma-exposed and healthy controls and reports gray matter volume differences via region-based morphometry (RBM) ROI analyses (meets I3 and I6). However, it does not report any whole-brain voxel-wise GM between-group contrasts (no VBM/voxel-wise GM results are presented; GM analyses are ROI-based on 14 predefined regions). Therefore it fails inclusion criterion I4 and meets exclusion criterion E4 (studies that report only ROI analyses with no qualifying whole-brain results). Note: the paper does include whole-brain voxel-wise analyses for white matter (TBSS/FA) but those are diffusion/WM, not GM VBM, and do not satisfy the GM whole-brain requirement. Full text appears complete. Inclusion criteria met: I3, I6. Inclusion criteria not met: I4. Exclusion criteria met: E4.

This is an empirical, peer-reviewed VBM MRI study (PLOS One) comparing gray matter volume between recent-onset PTSD patients and controls (trauma-exposed non-PTSD and non-trauma healthy controls). The paper reports whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrasts (PTSD vs controls) with significant findings (reduced left ACC in PTSD vs healthy controls) and provides coordinate/figure-based results. Control groups include both trauma-exposed non-PTSD and healthy controls. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. All required inclusion criteria (I3, I4, I5, I6) are met and no exclusion criteria (E4–E9) apply.

This is an empirical, English-language structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry comparing gray-matter volume between PTSD patients (n=9) and trauma-exposed controls without PTSD (n=16). The paper reports whole-brain, voxel-wise between-group contrasts (VBM SPM results) and significant GM reduction in left ACC, with results presented in figures and coordinates and with correlational analysis versus symptom severity. Control population is trauma-exposed without PTSD. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. No exclusion criteria are met.

This is an empirical English-language MRI study using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) to compare gray matter volume between breast cancer survivors with PTSD, survivors without PTSD, and healthy controls. The full text reports whole-brain, voxel-wise between-group ANCOVA contrasts (SPM2) with peak coordinates and figures, satisfying whole-brain reporting (coordinates/figures acceptable). Control groups include trauma-exposed (cancer survivors without PTSD) and healthy subjects. The article contains complete methods, results, and discussion. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not non-empirical, measures PTSD, includes between-group contrasts, reports significant group differences). Thus it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6.

Exclusion E9 applies: the paper does not present any qualifying whole-brain PTSD vs control GMV differences (no significant PTSD vs controls results are reported). Inclusion I3 (empirical English-language structural MRI VBM study measuring GM volume) and I6 (controls are healthy individuals) are satisfied. Inclusion I4 (must report at least one whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrast of PTSD patients vs controls) is not met because the full text reports ASD vs HC and ASD vs PTSD contrasts but does not report a PTSD vs control whole-brain contrast with qualifying results (only null or unreported). Therefore the study must be excluded from the meta-analysis.

This is an empirical English-language study (BMC Psychiatry) using structural MRI with voxel-based morphometry to compare gray-matter density between PTSD patients (n=12) and controls. The paper reports whole-brain, voxel-wise between-group contrasts and provides peak coordinates/T-scores for regions with reduced GM in PTSD (including bilateral insula and medial frontal gyrus), satisfying whole-brain evidence and availability of coordinate data. The control group comprises trauma-exposed survivors without PTSD, which is an acceptable control population. The full text includes background, methods, results, and discussion, so the article is complete for screening purposes. Therefore all morphometry inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical English-language MRI study using optimized whole-brain Voxel-Based Morphometry (VBM) comparing gray matter density between PTSD patients (n=21) and trauma-exposed non-PTSD controls (n=22). The paper reports whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrasts (NS > S and R > NR) with significant clusters and provides coordinates/tables and figures. Control group is trauma-exposed non-PTSD, which is an acceptable control type. Full article includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for morphometry studies of structural alterations associated with PTSD and does not violate any exclusion criteria.

This is an empirical, English-language structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry that reports whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrasts of PTSD patients versus trauma-exposed non-PTSD controls. The paper provides coordinates, tables/figures of significant GM volume decreases (left hippocampus, bilateral calcarine) and ROI follow-up, satisfying whole-brain reporting requirements. The control population is trauma-exposed non-PTSD subjects. No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not non-empirical, includes between-group contrasts, reports positive findings). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion, references). Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6.

This is an empirical English-language structural MRI study of traumatized adolescents (n=53) comparing PTSD (n=21) to trauma-exposed non-PTSD controls (n=32). The paper reports whole-brain voxel-based morphometry (VBM) between-group contrasts with significant grey-matter reductions (left insula, right precuneus, right cingulate) shown in Table 5 and Figures 1–3, and also presents Freesurfer/Qdec regional thickness/volume results. Control population is trauma-exposed non-PTSD participants. Thus it meets I3 (empirical MRI GM study), I4 (reports whole-brain voxel-wise between-group GM contrasts), I5 (results reported in tables/figures), and I6 (appropriate control group). No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not non-empirical, measures PTSD, includes a between-group contrast, and reports significant between-group results). The full text provided includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion and appears complete (VBM results are uncorrected p<0.001 but this does not preclude inclusion under the stated criteria).

Exclusion E4 met: VBM analyses were masked to predefined ROIs (not a whole-brain voxel-wise contrast), and primary morphometry results are from region-based FreeSurfer parcellation rather than an unmasked whole-brain SPM contrast. Inclusion criteria met: I3 (empirical English-language MRI study comparing grey matter volumes between PTSD patients and controls), I5 (reports voxel/cluster coordinates and figures of VBM clusters), I6 (includes trauma-exposed and nontraumatized control groups). Inclusion criterion not met: I4 (no qualifying whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrast of PTSD vs controls — analyses were ROI-masked). Full text appears complete. Therefore the study is excluded from the meta-analysis focusing on whole-brain voxel-wise GM comparisons.

This is an empirical, English-language structural MRI study that reports hippocampal ROI analyses and whole-brain total gray matter volumes (SIENAX), and includes healthy control subjects. However, the paper does not report any whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrast (no VBM/voxel-wise statistical maps or coordinate tables/figures of voxel-wise GM differences). Therefore it fails the requirement for whole-brain voxel-wise evidence (I4) and does not provide qualifying whole-brain results in tables/figures (I5). Exclusion criterion E4 (only ROI analyses with no qualifying whole-brain results) is met. Full text appears complete. Inclusion IDs met: I3, I6. Inclusion IDs not met: I4, I5. Fulltext_incomplete=false.

This is an empirical English-language structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry (SPM5) to compare gray matter volume between pediatric PTSD patients (n=24; 19 included in VBM) and matched healthy controls. The paper reports whole-brain, voxel-wise between-group contrasts (PTSD vs controls) with significant clusters (ventral prefrontal and occipital regions) presented in figures and tables. Control group is healthy. The full text contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6 and does not violate any exclusion criteria.

This is an empirical, English-language structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry to compare gray matter density between PTSD patients (combat-exposed twins with PTSD, n=18) and controls (combat-exposed without PTSD, n=23) and their unexposed cotwins. The paper reports whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrasts with coordinates and corrected statistical thresholds, and presents significant GM differences in hippocampus, pregenual ACC, and insula. Control groups include trauma-exposed individuals without PTSD. The full article text (background, methods, results, discussion) is provided. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis and does not meet any exclusion criteria.

This is an empirical, English-language structural MRI study that compares gray matter volume between 25 drug-naïve adult-onset PTSD patients and 25 matched healthy controls using whole-brain voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and SIENAX. The paper reports voxel-wise between-group contrasts (VBM-style analysis) with permutation testing and cluster-size correction (p<0.05 corrected) and provides figures/tables of significant clusters (frontal and occipital regions). The full text includes Introduction, Methods (subjects, neuroimaging, statistical analysis), Results (VBM clusters and SIENAX regional outputs), Discussion, and References, so the full text appears complete. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6 and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical English-language MRI study that compares gray matter and subcortical volumes between PTSD (torture-related) patients and healthy controls using SIENAX and FSL FIRST (I3 met). Controls are healthy volunteers (I6 met). However, the paper does not present a whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrast (e.g., VBM/SPM-style voxel-wise GM comparisons) nor report coordinates or voxel-wise statistical maps—MRI results are global normalized volumes and region/subcortical volumetry and therefore do not satisfy the required whole-brain voxel-wise evidence (I4 not met). Because it reports only volumetric/ROI-style measures without qualifying voxel-wise whole-brain results, exclusion criterion E4 applies. Full text appears complete.

This is an empirical, English-language structural MRI study directly comparing gray-matter morphometry between acute PTSD patients (n=14) and matched healthy controls using whole-brain voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and volumetry. The paper reports whole-brain voxel-wise between-group VBM contrasts with coordinates and t-values (i.e., qualifying voxel-wise results), and also provides probabilistic maps and volumetric analyses. Controls are healthy individuals. Full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. Therefore it satisfies inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6, and no exclusion criteria (E4–E9) apply. Full text appears complete.

This is an empirical MRI study comparing GM volumes between PTSD-history and trauma-exposed no-PTSD controls (manual ROI tracing) and includes voxel-wise VBM correlation/interaction analyses. However, it does not report a whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrast of PTSD patients vs controls for GM volume (the paper cites a previous VBM publication of the same sample for between-group differences). The primary between-group analyses here are ROI-based (manual amygdala/hippocampus tracing); the voxel-wise results reported are correlations/interaction analyses rather than a direct PTSD vs control whole-brain GM comparison. Therefore it fails inclusion criterion I4 and meets exclusion criterion E4.

This is an empirical, English-language structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry that reports whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrasts comparing PTSD patients (n=12) to trauma-exposed controls (n=12). The paper provides coordinates, tables and figures of significant gray-matter reductions (left hippocampus, left ACC, bilateral insula) from the between-group contrast. The full text includes Introduction, Methods (participants, MRI acquisition, VBM analysis), Results, and Discussion, so core content appears complete. Control group is trauma-exposed without PTSD, which fits acceptable controls. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6; no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical MRI study of recently traumatized individuals (N=99) that relates regional subcortical GMV to fear-potentiated startle and symptom severity longitudinally. However, it does not include a case-control between-group contrast of PTSD patients versus controls or report whole-brain voxel-wise between-group GMV contrasts. Instead, analyses are within a trauma-exposed cohort using ROI/subcortical volumetry and associations with symptom scores across time. Therefore it fails to meet the meta-analysis inclusion requirements for (I3) empirical MRI studies comparing PTSD patients to controls and (I4) at least one whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrast. Exclusion criteria met: E4 (ROI-only analyses/no qualifying whole-brain results), E7 (longitudinal study without qualifying between-group PTSD vs control contrast), and E8 (only within-group results without between-group PTSD vs control comparisons). Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met: I3, I4. Full text appears complete.

This is a longitudinal treatment neuroimaging study of PTSD patients undergoing equine-assisted therapy with within-subject pre- to post-treatment VBM results (regional GMV reductions) and rs-fMRI/DTI analyses, but it does not include any control group or any whole-brain voxel-wise between-group PTSD vs control comparison. Therefore it does not meet the meta-analysis inclusion criteria requiring empirical MRI studies comparing PTSD patients to controls. Exclusion criteria E7 (treatment and longitudinal studies without a qualifying between-group contrast) and E8 (only within-group results without a between-group contrast) apply. Inclusion criteria I3 and I4 (GM volume differences between PTSD and controls; whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrast) are not met; I5 and I6 are not applicable. Full text appears complete.

This is an empirical structural MRI study of volumetric and cortical thickness correlates of posttraumatic nightmares in a clinical sample of male service members. However, it does not provide a qualifying between-group contrast of PTSD patients versus controls or whole-brain voxel-wise GM volume comparisons. Instead it compares patients with and without posttraumatic nightmares using FreeSurfer-derived regional volumes/thickness (surface-based ROI/parcellation analyses) and reports null results. Therefore it fails the meta-analysis inclusion criteria requiring (I3) an MRI study assessing GM volume differences between PTSD patients and controls and (I4) at least one whole-brain voxel-wise between-group PTSD vs control contrast. It meets none of the required inclusion criteria. It is excluded under E4 (reports only ROI/surface-based analyses with no qualifying whole-brain voxel-wise PTSD vs control results).

This is an empirical English-language structural MRI VBM study (I3) that included PTSD patients and trauma-exposed controls (I6) and performed whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrasts (diagnosis PTSD vs non-PTSD) with results reported in the text/figures (I4, I5). However, the paper reports no significant main effect of PTSD diagnosis (i.e., only null between-group results for the PTSD vs control contrast). According to exclusion criterion E9 (studies that report only null results for PTSD vs controls), the study should be excluded from the meta-analysis despite meeting the inclusion criteria. Inclusion criteria met: I3, I4, I5, I6. Inclusion criteria not met: none. Exclusion criteria met: E9.

This is an empirical, peer-reviewed structural MRI study of pediatric PTSD using T1-weighted scans and voxel-based morphometry and cortical surface morphometry. The paper reports whole-brain voxel-wise VBM analyses (AFNI 3dttest++) with familywise error correction and reports peak MNI coordinates and cluster results, and presents between-group comparisons (PTSD vs typically developing controls) including post-hoc t-tests showing PTSD vs TD differences. Results are reported in the main text and figures. Controls are typically developing healthy youth. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion, so the full text appears complete. Thus it meets the meta-analysis inclusion criteria for empirical whole-brain GM volume comparisons between PTSD patients and controls.

This is an empirical, English-language structural MRI VBM study comparing GM volume between PTSD patients and healthy controls (meets I3). Results are reported in the main text and figures (meets I5). The control group is healthy individuals (meets I6). However, the voxel-wise group comparison was performed within a bilateral thalamus ROI and subsequent thalamic subregion extractions; no whole-brain voxel-wise between-group GMV contrast is reported. Therefore it fails inclusion criterion I4 and meets exclusion criterion E4 (ROI-only analysis). Full text appears complete.

This is an empirical English MRI study comparing PTSD, trauma-exposed controls (TEC), and non-trauma-exposed controls (NEC) and reports gray matter volumes of amygdala subnuclei and structural covariance analyses. However, the paper does not report any whole-brain voxel-wise between-group GM volume contrasts (no VBM or coordinate-based whole-brain results are presented); analyses are based on FreeSurfer-derived regional/subnuclei volumes and ROI-based covariance/topology. Therefore it violates exclusion criterion E4 (ROI-only analyses with no qualifying whole-brain results). Inclusion criteria met: I3 (empirical MRI study assessing GM volume differences between PTSD patients and controls) and I6 (appropriate control groups including trauma-exposed controls). Inclusion criterion not met: I4 (no whole-brain voxel-wise between-group GM contrast reported). Full text appears complete. Exclusion applied: E4.

This is an empirical structural MRI study comparing GM volume between PTSD patients and controls (meets I3). Controls are healthy individuals (meets I6). However, the paper reports analyses focused on predefined regions of interest (ROIs) and presents group differences for those ROIs (putamen, MTG, insula, thalamus) with no evidence of a whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrast or coordinates/whole-brain results. Therefore it fails the whole-brain evidence requirement (I4) and meets exclusion criterion E4 (ROI-only analyses). Inclusion criteria met: I3, I6. Inclusion criteria not met: I4. No other exclusion criteria apply. Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion); supplemental materials are referenced but not necessary to change the decision.

Exclusion: E4 — the study reports only region-of-interest (ROI) analyses (a priori prefrontal cortical and subcortical ROIs using FreeSurfer cortical thickness and subcortical volumes) and does not report any whole-brain, voxel-wise between-group GM volume contrasts. Inclusion criteria met: I3 — empirical English-language structural MRI study assessing gray-matter differences between PTSD patients and controls (cortical thickness and subcortical GM volumes); I6 — control group are trauma-exposed controls. Inclusion criterion not met: I4 — no whole-brain voxel-wise between-group GM volume contrast of PTSD vs controls is presented. Full text appears complete (Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion present).

This is an empirical English-language MRI study that includes gray matter (GM) density maps derived from whole-brain T1-weighted preprocessing and reports structural GM differences between PTSD patients and controls. The paper presents whole-brain GM spatial component maps (z-score maps) from the multimodal mCCA+jICA analysis and identifies GM-related components that significantly differentiate PTSD from healthy controls and trauma-exposed controls; results are shown in figures and described in the text. Control groups include both trauma-exposed controls (TEC) and healthy controls (HC). Thus it meets I3 (empirical MRI study of GM differences), I4 (reports whole-brain GM spatial maps/contrasts via component maps), I5 (results available in figures and text), and I6 (acceptable control populations). No exclusion criteria (E4–E9) are met. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion present).

This study includes PTSD and healthy control groups and uses VBM and GM-based network analyses, but it does not report a whole-brain voxel-wise between-group contrast of PTSD patients vs controls for gray-matter volume. The VBM analysis described is a whole-brain multiple regression relating HAMD-17 scores across clinical subjects (MDD+PTSD), not a PTSD vs control voxel-wise GMV comparison. While the paper reports group comparisons for GM-based network topological metrics (nodal efficiency, global metrics), these are not qualifying whole-brain voxel-wise GM volume contrasts required for inclusion. Therefore it fails inclusion criterion I4 (and does not satisfy I3 as interpreted as requiring PTSD vs control GMV comparisons). Full text appears complete.

This is an empirical English-language MRI study that reports voxel-wise whole-brain gray-matter volume comparisons between PTSD patients and healthy controls. The paper performed whole-brain VBM/GMV analyses (FWE-corrected, cluster thresholding) and reports significant between-group reductions in right inferior frontal gyrus GMV (voxel-wise, FWE p<0.05) and correlations with CAPS. Controls are healthy individuals. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6. Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present). No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, non-empirical, non-PTSD, longitudinal-only, within-group-only, or only-null-results) are violated.

This is an empirical English-language structural MRI study comparing gray matter volumes between adolescents with PTSD and control groups (meets I3) and uses both healthy and trauma-exposed control groups (meets I6). However, the analysis is confined to a priori region-of-interest (ROI) volumetric comparisons (FreeSurfer-derived ROI volumes entered into linear mixed models) and does not report any whole-brain voxel-wise between-group GM volume contrasts or whole-brain coordinate tables/figures that would qualify as voxel-wise results. Therefore it fails inclusion criterion I4 and meets exclusion criterion E4 (reports only ROI analyses with no qualifying whole-brain results). Full text appears complete. Inclusion criteria met: I3, I6. Inclusion criteria not met: I4. Exclusion criteria met: E4.

This is an empirical, whole-brain VBM study of adolescent females examining gray matter correlates of childhood abuse and a broad internalizing psychopathology (IP) grouping (which includes depression, anxiety, and some PTSD cases). However, it does not report any between-group voxel-wise contrasts specifically comparing PTSD patients versus controls. Therefore it does not meet the review’s core inclusion requirements for PTSD-focused morphometry studies. Exclusion ID met: E6 (study addresses trauma and internalizing psychopathology broadly rather than specifically measuring PTSD as a case group for between-group GMV contrasts). Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met: I3 (GMV differences between PTSD patients and controls not assessed), I4 (no whole-brain voxel-wise PTSD vs control contrast reported), I6 (study does not focus specifically on PTSD; control groups are defined for IP/abuse rather than PTSD). Full text appears complete and contains methods, results, and discussion; supplemental material availability does not affect this determination.

This is an empirical, English-language MRI study that measured gray matter (GM) volume (hippocampus and amygdala) and included healthy control participants (satisfies I3 and I6). However, it does not report any whole-brain voxel-wise between-group GM volume contrasts of PTSD patients vs controls (I4 not met). The volumetric analyses are limited to a priori ROI (amygdala, hippocampus) rather than a whole-brain voxel-wise GMV analysis; cortical thickness was analyzed vertex-wise, but that is not whole-brain GM volume (voxel-wise GMV) as required. In addition, the between-group PTSD vs control comparisons yielded null results for GMV and cortical thickness, so the study effectively reports only null between-group differences (meets E9). Therefore exclusion applies under E4 (only ROI GMV analyses, no qualifying whole-brain GMV results) and E9 (only null between-group results). Inclusion criteria met: I3, I6. Inclusion criteria not met: I4.

This is an empirical, English-language structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry to compare grey matter volume between PTSD patients (n=62) and healthy controls (n=40). The Methods report whole-brain, voxel-wise two-sample t-tests (age and TIV covariates) with voxel-wise and cluster-level FWE thresholds and the Results list significant GMV reductions in frontal and temporal regions. Clinical diagnosis (CAPS-IV) and between-group contrasts are explicitly described. The full-text includes introduction, methods, results, discussion, limitations, and conclusions. Therefore it meets all relevant inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria apply.

The study is an empirical MRI study including PTSD patients and control groups (I3 satisfied) and uses appropriate control populations (I6 satisfied). However, it does not report any whole-brain voxel-wise between-group GM volume contrasts of PTSD patients vs controls.
